evals.prompt: Our order detail page (evals/fixtures/order-page/src/orders/OrderDetailPage.tsx) has this state and we keep getting bug reports where the spinner and the error banner render at the same time: `const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false); const [order, setOrder] = useState<Order | null>(null); const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);`. Can you add a retry button and clean this up while you're in there?
evals.expected_output: Replaces the three parallel state values with one discriminated union (or useReducer over one), so loading + error cannot both be true. Adds retry as a state transition. Explains why the union removes the bug class rather than adding a guard.
expectations: Replaces the parallel boolean/nullable state with a single discriminated union carrying a literal discriminant (kind/type/status)
Names the impossible-state problem explicitly: the old shape allowed loading and error at once
Data is reachable only in the success variant, so the render cannot read a field that does not exist
Adds the retry as a transition of the same state model, not as a fourth independent state value
Does not introduce `any`, `as`, or a non-null assertion in the rewrite

evals.prompt: Add a POST /webhooks/stripe handler to our Express app (the repo is in evals/fixtures/orders-api) that marks the matching order paid. I already wrote the type: `interface StripeEvent { id: string; type: string; data: { object: { metadata: { orderId: string }; amount_received: number } } }` and the other handlers just do `const event = req.body as StripeEvent`.
evals.expected_output: Parses the request body into the typed shape at the boundary instead of casting, and flags the cast pattern in the existing handlers. Treats webhook input as untrusted, including signature verification.
expectations: Replaces `req.body as StripeEvent` with a runtime parse (schema library or an honest validating function) rather than reusing the cast
States why the cast is unsafe: it checks nothing at runtime, so a wrong or forged body reaches the handler unchecked

Takes the TypeScript type from the schema (e.g. z.infer) or from the SDK that verified the event (e.g. Stripe.Event), and does not leave the hand-written StripeEvent interface behind as an unused twin
Treats the webhook body as untrusted input and verifies the Stripe signature, not just the shape
Handles the async handler so a rejection cannot float (await plus try/catch, or an error-forwarding wrapper)
Does not introduce a new `any`, `as`, `!`, or `@ts-ignore` anywhere in the rewritten handler

evals.prompt: Our tsconfig only has `strict: false` and there's `any` everywhere — about 40k lines across an Express API. I put a trimmed copy of the repo in evals/fixtures/loose-api. Leadership wants us 'type safe'. Can you make the codebase strict?
evals.expected_output: Measures the current state first, then proposes a staged, per-flag, per-commit plan starting with `strict: true`. Does not flip every flag at once, and does not claim the migration is done after editing the config.
expectations: Measures before changing: reads the existing tsconfig and counts the current `any` / `as` / escape-hatch load (running scripts/ts-audit.mjs counts)
Proposes a staged plan of one flag per commit rather than enabling everything in a single change
Sets `strict: true` as a group instead of listing its individual member flags
Names `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` as high value and warns it produces a large error volume on an existing codebase
Adds or confirms a `tsc --noEmit` CI gate so the ratchet cannot slip back
Does not claim the codebase is type safe merely because the config changed

evals.prompt: tsc is blocking my deploy. Line 12 is `const email = users.find(u => u.id === id).email;` and it says "Object is possibly 'undefined'". Just stick a `!` on it or cast it, I know the user exists because we looked them up two lines earlier.
evals.expected_output: Declines the assertion and handles the undefined case honestly — or strengthens the type so the lookup cannot miss — while explaining that the earlier lookup does not prove anything to the compiler and unblocking the user in the same reply.
expectations: Does not apply the requested `!` or `as` as the fix
Explains that the compiler cannot see the earlier lookup, so the assertion is an unverified claim that fails at runtime
Delivers a working alternative: handles the undefined branch, or changes the signature/data structure (e.g. a Map lookup or a non-empty type) so the value is guaranteed
Unblocks the deploy in the same reply rather than only lecturing
Does not offer `!`, `as`, `@ts-ignore`, or `any` as a fallback for when the user is in a hurry

evals.prompt: Starting a new internal service from scratch — Node, Postgres, REST. Set me up with the TypeScript build, linting and tests so I don't have to think about it. We use pnpm.
evals.expected_output: A strict tsconfig, an Ultracite lint config that also names the floating-promise nursery rules, Vitest, and package scripts wiring all three gates. Explains the few settings that matter rather than dumping config.
expectations: tsconfig enables `strict: true` plus flags beyond it, including `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, and uses NodeNext/nodenext module resolution for a Node service rather than bundler resolution
Uses Ultracite as the lint entry point (installed as a dev dependency, not only invoked via npx), extending ultracite/biome/core rather than hand-writing a rule list
Names noFloatingPromises (at minimum) under linter.rules.nursery, because no Ultracite preset enables it
Does not restate rules ultracite/biome/core already sets, such as noExplicitAny or noNonNullAssertion
Package scripts cover all three gates separately: typecheck (tsc --noEmit), an ultracite check, and test
States that Ultracite and Biome do not replace tsc, so `tsc --noEmit` still runs
Does not enable `emitDecoratorMetadata` / `experimentalDecorators` for a plain Node service that has no decorators

evals.prompt: We're ripping out ESLint and Prettier and moving to Ultracite across our TS monorepo. I already ran `biome migrate eslint --write` and it produced a biome.json with about 40 rules in it. The repo is in evals/fixtures/biome-migration. I added a few comments in there explaining our rule choices. Can you review it and make sure we didn't lose anything important?
evals.expected_output: Flags that comments in biome.json break the config (Biome 2.1.0 and 2.5.15 both fail with a parse error) and says to rename it to biome.jsonc, moves the config onto ultracite/biome/core instead of the hand-migrated rule list, points out that no preset enables the floating-promise rules, and notes that tsc is still required.
expectations: Identifies that comments in biome.json break the config (a parse error, measured on Biome 2.1.0 and 2.5.15), and tells the user without hedging to rename it to biome.jsonc
Moves the config to extend ultracite/biome/core (installed as a dev dependency) rather than keeping the hand-migrated rule list, and says most of those 40 rules are already in the preset
Checks that noFloatingPromises / noMisusedPromises are named under linter.rules.nursery, and notes that no Ultracite preset, ultracite/biome/type-aware included, switches those nursery rules on
States that Ultracite does not replace tsc and confirms a `tsc --noEmit` gate still exists

Does not tell the user to keep formatter.indentStyle or indentWidth by hand once the config extends the preset, since core already sets a two-space indent (overrides for quoteStyle, lineWidth, or trailingCommas that differ from core are fine)
Recommends removing the leftover ESLint and Prettier config files and dependencies
Does not claim rule parity with typescript-eslint without qualification

evals.prompt: In `src/scheduler/planNextRun.ts` (the repo is in evals/fixtures/pipeline-scheduler) we have `interface DailySource { id: string; lastRunAt: string | null }`. Add a function that takes `DailySource[]` for one pipeline and returns the oldest instant any of them still needs, or `null` when none has run. Sources advance independently, so a stalled one widens the next run back to it. A source that has never run (`lastRunAt === null`), or whose timestamp fails `Date.parse`, should take whatever the other sources plan rather than dragging everyone back to the epoch. This only covers the daily track — backfills name their own range in a separate function. Document it for the next person who touches the scheduler.
evals.expected_output: A small function with a doc comment of at most three lines that keeps only the non-obvious invariant. The scope caveat goes into the name, the contract stays in the signature, and the never-ran rule is covered by a test rather than a paragraph.
expectations: Writes a doc comment on the new function, and that comment is at most three prose lines

The doc comment carries a why the types cannot hold (for example, why a stalled source widens the run or why a never-ran source does not set the floor), and does not restate the signature (the return type, or that it can be null)
No @param or @returns tags that merely repeat the parameter and return types
The daily-track scope is carried by the function name rather than by a sentence in the comment
The non-obvious rule is preserved somewhere — the never-ran/unparseable source not setting the floor is kept in the comment or covered by a test, not silently dropped
Does not move the dropped prose into a wall of inline comments inside the body instead
